repo.description:
### Summary

**This is not a new vulnerability and I am not claiming it as one.** GHSA-7r6p-v9gw-pwc8 already names `apps/dokploy/server/wss/listen-deployment.ts` in its "Vulnerable handlers" list. What is new is that the fix skipped that file, and it is still unauthorized at `v0.30.2` - four weeks after publication.

Any authenticated organization member - with no role, no service grant and no docker permission - can open `/listen-deployment` and stream the contents of any file under `/etc/dokploy`, including the SSH private key Dokploy uses to reach the Docker host, Traefik certificate private keys, other applications' `.env` files and compose files. Recovering the host SSH key is host compromise.

Note also that GHSA-7r6p-v9gw-pwc8 records its affected range as `<= 0.29.8`, which reads as "fixed after 0.29.8". For this handler that is not the case, so users reading that advisory would conclude they are patched when they are not.

### Details

Commit `68f5afae` (2026-07-19), *"fix(security): authorize docker/terminal WebSocket handlers"*, introduced `apps/dokploy/server/wss/authorize.ts` and applied it to exactly four handlers:

```
apps/dokploy/__test__/wss/authorize.test.ts          | 80 ++++++++++
apps/dokploy/server/wss/authorize.ts                 | 69 ++++++++
apps/dokploy/server/wss/docker-container-logs.ts     |  6 ++
apps/dokploy/server/wss/docker-container-terminal.ts |  6 ++
apps/dokploy/server/wss/docker-stats.ts              |  6 ++
apps/dokploy/server/wss/terminal.ts                  |  6 ++
```

`listen-deployment.ts` is not among them, despite being registered on the adjacent line of `server.ts` (`:51` vs `:52`). It has received **zero commits since the advisory was published**:

```
$ git log --since=2026-07-19 -- apps/dokploy/server/wss/listen-deployment.ts
(no output)
```

At `v0.30.2`, grepping that file for `checkPermission|hasPermission|checkServiceAccess|canAccess|role|accessedServices` returns nothing. Its only check remains authentication:

```ts
const { user, session } = await validateRequest(req);
...
if (!user || !session) { ws.close(); return; }
```

Compare the guarded sibling, `docker-container-logs.ts:79-82`:

```ts
if (!(await canAccessDockerOverWss(user, session, serverId, serviceId))) {
  ws.close(4003, "Not authorized");
  return;
}
```

On the local branch (no `serverId`) `listen-deployment` has not even an organization check. The remote branch does compare `server.organizationId !== session.activeOrganizationId`, so only the local path is fully unscoped.

**What the one remaining check permits.** `readValidDirectory` (`packages/server/src/wss/utils.ts:39-55`) is well built - charset allowlist, `path.resolve` before comparison, `resolvedBase + path.sep` to defeat the sibling-prefix bug. It is **not** bypassable and this is not a traversal report. But it constrains the path only to `BASE_PATH`, and `paths()` (`packages/server/src/constants/index.ts:96-119`) places `SSH_PATH`, `CERTIFICATES_PATH`, `APPLICATIONS_PATH` and `COMPOSE_PATH` *under* that same base.

`tail -n +1 -f <path>` prints the whole file before following, so the socket returns full contents. `spawn("tail", ["-n","+1","-f", logPath])` uses an argv array with no shell - there is **no command injection here** and I claim none.

**Suggested fix.** Apply the guard the other four handlers received. Since deployment logs belong to a service, the natural call is the service-scoped branch `canAccessDockerOverWss` already implements:

```ts
if (!(await canAccessDockerOverWss(user, session, serverId, serviceId))) {
  ws.close(4003, "Not authorized");
  return;
}
```

That needs a `serviceId` (or `applicationId`/`deploymentId`) parameter with the log path resolved from it server-side, rather than accepting a caller-supplied absolute path at all - which removes the file-scope problem entirely. More durably: authorization here is applied by enumerating handlers rather than at the socket-upgrade boundary, which is why this one was missed; a single upgrade-time gate would make the next handler secure by default.

### PoC

**On a self-hosted instance.** Invite a user as a plain `member` with no service access, capture their `better-auth.session_token`, then:

```bash
websocat "ws://TARGET:3000/listen-deployment?logPath=%2Fetc%2Fdokploy%2Fssh%2Fauto_generated-dokploy-local" \
  -H "Cookie: better-auth.session_token=<MEMBER_COOKIE>"
# -> the SSH private key is streamed over the socket
```

Any path under `/etc/dokploy` works, e.g. `/etc/dokploy/traefik/dynamic/certificates/<name>.key`, `/etc/dokploy/applications/<app>/code/.env`, `/etc/dokploy/compose/<project>/docker-compose.yml`.

**Confirmed directly against the handler.** I ran your real `setupDeploymentLogsWebSocketServer` and your real `readValidDirectory` with a real `ws` client over a real HTTP upgrade, against a clone at `v0.30.2`. Only `validateRequest` was stubbed - that is the whole point of the finding: the claim is that authentication is the only check performed. The simulated member carries no role, no service grant and no docker permission:

```
=== CONTROL 1: NOT authenticated ===
  no session,  ssh key     closed (code 1005), no data

=== CONTROL 2: authenticated, path OUTSIDE /etc/dokploy ===
  member,      /etc/passwd closed (code 4000), no data

=== CONTROL 3: authenticated, a genuine deployment log (intended use) ===
  member,      app.log     STREAMED -> "ordinary deployment log line"

=== EXPLOIT: same low-privilege member, host SSH private key ===
  member,      SSH KEY     STREAMED -> "-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----\nZT-CANARY-..."
```

The three controls are deliberate: **1** proves authentication is genuinely enforced, so the stub is not disabling the handler's logic; **2** proves `readValidDirectory` is real and firing; **3** proves intended use still works. Only the file path differs between control 3 and the exploit - nothing about the caller changes.

A second run of the same validator confirms the scope: `/etc/dokploy/traefik/dynamic/certificates/cert.key`, `/etc/dokploy/applications/victim-app/code/.env` and `/etc/dokploy/compose/victim/docker-compose.yml` are all ALLOWED, while `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/dokploy/../etc/passwd` and `/etc/dokploy-evil/secrets` are correctly blocked.

### Impact

Missing authorization (CWE-862) on a WebSocket endpoint that reads arbitrary files from Dokploy's data directory.

Any authenticated member of any organization on a self-hosted instance - including one deliberately granted no service permissions - can read:

- `/etc/dokploy/ssh/auto_generated-dokploy-local` - the SSH key Dokploy uses to reach the Docker host. Recovering it is **host compromise**, which is why Scope is Changed.
- per-server SSH private keys for every remote server the instance manages
- Traefik TLS certificate private keys
- other applications' source and `.env` files, and compose files

This is the same outcome GHSA-7r6p-v9gw-pwc8 already describes; it simply was not closed for this handler. The remote (`serverId`) branch does enforce organization ownership, so the fully unscoped path is the local one. Whether a given key file exists depends on the deployment - `setupLocalServerSSHKey` generates `auto_generated-dokploy-local` on first use of the host terminal.
repo.summary: Incomplete fix of GHSA-7r6p-v9gw-pwc8: listen-deployment.ts is named in that advisory but was never remediated - any authenticated member can stream host SSH private keys
